title: Before the Sanhedrin, and a Night Ride to Caesarea
summary: Paul stands before the Jewish high council, clashes with the high priest, and splits the council by declaring that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection. That night the Lord tells him he must testify in Rome. When more than forty men swear to kill him, Paul's nephew exposes the plot, and the Roman commander sends Paul under heavy guard to Governor Felix in Caesarea.
story: Paul came to Jerusalem knowing he faced chains (Acts 20:22-23, 21:10-14). In Acts 21 he was nearly killed by a crowd in the temple courts and rescued by Roman soldiers; in Acts 22 he told his story of meeting the risen Jesus and escaped a flogging by stating that he was a Roman citizen. Now the commander, trying to learn what the charge is, brings him before the Sanhedrin. The chapter turns the book's last movement toward Rome. Jesus had promised that his followers would be his witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8), and here the Lord himself tells Paul that his testimony in Jerusalem will be followed by testimony in Rome. From this point on every hearing, delay, and danger is part of the road there.
historical:
The Sanhedrin was the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders, and scribes under the presiding high priest, with authority over religious and many civil matters under Roman oversight. The high priest here, Ananias son of Nedebaeus, held office from about AD 47 to about 59. The Jewish historian Josephus remembers him as wealthy, greedy, and violent, and reports that he was killed by Jewish insurgents at the outbreak of the war with Rome in AD 66.

The Roman commander, whose name we learn from his letter, was Claudius Lysias, a tribune in charge of the cohort (a unit nominally of a thousand men) stationed in the Antonia fortress overlooking the temple. He had bought his citizenship (Acts 22:28), and his name suggests he took it in the reign of the emperor Claudius. The governor he writes to is Antonius Felix, who governed Judea in the 50s AD (the start of his term is usually placed about AD 52). Roman writers remembered Felix as a former slave who rose through the influence of his brother Pallas at the imperial court, and as harsh in office. The escort's route ran northwest from Jerusalem to Antipatris, a town about thirty-five to forty miles away, then on across the coastal plain to Caesarea, the Roman capital of the province.
cultural:
Paul's appeal to the Sanhedrin's divisions depends on real differences. The Sadducees were drawn largely from the priestly aristocracy; they rejected the resurrection of the dead and, as Luke notes, belief in angels and spirits. The Pharisees were a popular lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law, and they expected the resurrection at the end of the age. When Paul says he is a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection, he is not inventing a side issue. For him the whole dispute turns on the claim that God has raised Jesus, the first fruits of that hope.

Other details reflect Roman practice. An oath not to eat or drink until a deed was done bound the swearer under a curse, and Luke uses a verb (anathematizo) that means exactly that. The commander's letter follows the standard form of the time, sender, recipient, greeting, and then the business, and it quietly improves his own part: he says he rescued Paul after learning he was a Roman, when in fact he learned it only as Paul was about to be flogged. The massive escort, some four hundred and seventy men, leaving at the third hour of the night (about nine in the evening), shows how seriously he took the threat and how much trouble a dead Roman citizen could cause him. At Caesarea Paul was held in the palace Herod the Great had built, which now served as the governor's headquarters.
literary: Luke builds the chapter in two panels joined by the Lord's night visit. The first panel (verses 1-10) is a courtroom scene that never reaches a verdict; it collapses into shouting, as the riot of chapter 21 did, and ends with Paul hauled away by soldiers. The second (verses 12-35) is a suspense story: an oath, a plot, a boy who overhears, a private word with the commander, and an escape by night. The center is verse 11, where the Lord stands by Paul and says, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.” The word must (dei) is the same one Luke uses for the divine necessity that governed Jesus's own road to the cross. The inserted letter (verses 26-30) also gives Luke's readers a Roman official's verdict: no charge worthy of death or imprisonment, a refrain that will return.

outline.t: The Lord's word: you must testify in Rome
More than forty men swear to kill Paul
The escort and Claudius Lysias's letter
By night to Antipatris and Caesarea

doctrines.note: God's care for Paul comes through ordinary means: a nephew in the right place, a commander willing to listen, and a Roman bureaucracy protecting a citizen. The Lord's promise in verse 11 does not remove danger; it sets the danger inside a purpose.

Paul names the resurrection of the dead as the hope for which he is on trial. The Christian hope is not merely survival of the soul but bodily resurrection, and Paul sees Jesus's resurrection as the beginning of what Israel hoped for.

Paul accuses the high priest of breaking the law by ordering him struck without a verdict, and then submits to the law himself by citing Exodus 22:28 about respect for rulers. Both men claim the law; Paul lets it judge him too.

words.note: Suneidesis, conscience: the inner awareness that judges one's own conduct. Paul uses the word often in his letters. His claim in verse 1 is not sinlessness (he elsewhere calls himself a former persecutor) but that he has lived before God with integrity as he understood it, including in following Jesus.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. In Jewish hope it meant the raising of the dead at the end of the age. The early church preached that this end-time event had already begun with Jesus, which is why the word could split a council.

Anathematizo, to bind under a curse. The conspirators call down a curse on themselves if they fail. The same family of words gives anathema, something devoted to destruction. Luke does not say what became of the forty men after their plot failed.
Tharseo, to take courage or be of good cheer. Jesus speaks this word to frightened people in the Gospels, and here the risen Lord speaks it to a prisoner. It is courage given, not summoned.

christ: Paul's hearing echoes Jesus's own. Jesus too stood before the Sanhedrin and a high priest, was struck on the face (John 18:22-23), and was handed to a Roman governor who found no basis for a charge. Luke tells the stories in parallel so that the reader sees the disciple walking the road of his Lord. But the chapter also shows who Christ is now: not a dead teacher whose followers remember him, but the living Lord who stands beside a prisoner at night, knows his future, and directs his mission. The resurrection Paul names in verse 6 is the reason the Lord can stand near him in verse 11.

hard.q: Why did Paul insult the high priest, and was his appeal to the Pharisees a clever trick?
hard.a:
Paul's words to Ananias are sharp, and his response when rebuked, that he did not know Ananias was high priest, has puzzled readers. Some think Paul, long absent from Jerusalem, did not recognize him in an informal meeting called by a Roman officer. Some point to possible poor eyesight (compare Galatians 4:15, 6:11). Others read the reply as irony: a man who orders a prisoner struck in defiance of the law does not act like a high priest. Many think Paul, having spoken in anger, simply recognized he had been wrong and submitted to Scripture. Luke does not settle it.

As for verse 6, some readers see a tactic to divide his opponents. That is part of what happens, but the claim itself is sincere and central. Paul really was a Pharisee by training, and the resurrection really was the heart of his message (Acts 24:15, 26:6-8). He exposes the fact that the council itself could not agree on the very hope his gospel proclaimed.

questions: Paul says he has lived before God in good conscience. What would it take for you to say that honestly, and where would you hesitate?
God protects Paul through a nephew and a Roman officer rather than a miracle. Where have you seen God work through ordinary people and institutions?
The Lord tells Paul to take courage without removing the danger. How does a promise about the future change the way someone faces a present threat?
